entities.summary:
This ancient practice of studying celestial objects and phenomena in the cosmos is rooted in human curiosity about the natural world. The earliest recorded astronomical observations date back to Mesopotamia around 2000 BCE, where civilizations such as the Sumerians and Babylonians developed sophisticated systems for tracking planetary movements and predicting lunar eclipses. These early astronomers made significant contributions to our understanding of astronomy, including the discovery of several constellations and the development of arithmetic methods for calculating astronomical tables. The ancient Greeks later built upon these achievements, making key discoveries such as the solar system's structure and the existence of comets.

Astronomy has had a profound impact on human culture and society, influencing art, literature, and religion. The study of celestial bodies has also driven technological innovation, from the development of telescopes to space exploration. Today, astronomy continues to expand our knowledge of the universe, with ongoing research in fields such as exoplanetary science and cosmology.

The legacy of astronomy can be seen in many modern technologies, including GPS systems, satellite communications, and weather forecasting. The field has also had a profound impact on our understanding of the universe, from the discovery of dark matter to the detection of gravitational waves. As we continue to explore the cosmos, we are reminded of the significance of human curiosity and the power of scientific inquiry.

Astronomy's influence on human history is exemplified by the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle, who wrote extensively on the subject of celestial bodies and their movements. The discovery of Pluto in 1930 marked a significant turning point in astronomy, as it challenged our understanding of the solar system's structure and led to a greater appreciation for the diversity of celestial objects.

Key lasting impacts include: Influenced intellectual traditions and cultural development.", "summary": "Astronomy is the natural science of celestial objects — stars, planets, moons, comets, asteroids, galaxies, and the universe as a whole — studying their positions, motions, physical properties, chemical composition, and origins through observation and theoretical analysis. It is the oldest of the natural sciences, with its roots in the naked-eye sky observations of ancient Mesopotamia, Egypt, Greece, India, China, and the pre-Columbian Americas, all of which developed systematic astronomical records and calendrical calculations thousands of years before the telescope existed. The regularity and grandeur of celestial phenomena — the seasonal cycle, the lunar calendar, the rising and setting of planets, the predictability of eclipses — made astronomy both practically essential (for agriculture, navigation, and timekeeping) and the paradigmatic domain of human attempts to understand the mathematical order of the cosmos.

The astronomical revolution of the 16th–17th centuries was one of the most consequential transformations in intellectual history: Copernicus's heliocentric model (De Revolutionibus, 1543) displaced the Earth from the centre of the cosmos; Brahe's precise naked-eye observations provided the data; Kepler's laws of planetary motion (1609–1619) described the elliptical orbits; Galileo's telescopic observations (1609) confirmed the Copernican system; and Newton's Principia Mathematica (1687) provided the gravitational mechanics that explained why planets move as they do. This sequence — the Copernican Revolution — is the archetypal scientific revolution, the model for how paradigms shift, and the event that established the authority of mathematical-empirical natural science over traditional theological cosmology.

Modern astronomy encompasses a vast range of sub-disciplines — planetary astronomy, stellar astronomy, galactic astronomy, cosmology, astrobiology — and observes the universe across the entire electromagnetic spectrum (radio, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma-ray) as well as through gravitational wave detection (LIGO, 2015) and neutrino astronomy.
